requirements.requirement: /srv/drop exists as a shared writable directory (world-writable, root-owned) on node1
requirements.summary: cmd-35a0be95f9d84d98 shows /srv/drop created with mode 1777 (drwxrwxrwt) owned root:root, directly observed via ls -ld.

requirements.requirement: Multiple users can write/create files in the shared directory
requirements.summary: Two test users (dropuser1, dropuser2) both successfully created files in /srv/drop, confirmed via ls -l output.

requirements.requirement: Users cannot remove or overwrite files owned by other users in the directory (sticky-bit protection)
requirements.summary: dropuser2's attempt to rm and truncate dropuser1's file both failed with 'Operation not permitted'/'Permission denied', directly demonstrating sticky-bit enforcement.

requirements.requirement: Configuration persists across a service/system disruption (restart) with recovered state and behavior
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id and healthy /srv/drop state captured (cmd-0d4e3ddfb2a94368), reboot acknowledged and connection loss/reconnect observed (cmd-6789226f50b045e1, cmd-884198fe8c204dd3, cmd-76958e132d5f4101), post-restart boot_id differs confirming actual reboot (cmd-97f429cfeb3c47af), and post-reboot re-verification shows /srv/drop still 1777 root:root with sticky-bit cross-user delete still blocked (cmd-a038126a203c40a9). Fixed lifecycle snapshots independently corroborate the boot-identity change.

overall_summary: The executor created /srv/drop with mode 1777 root:root and directly demonstrated, via a two-user test, that shared writes succeed while cross-user delete/overwrite is blocked by the sticky bit — both before and after a full node restart with a verified boot-identity change. All material outcomes of the task are satisfied with direct evidence, and the independent provider-wide restart protocol was executed cleanly with matching pre/post boot identities from the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Test artifacts (users and files) were created and removed in a bounded, purposeful way with no residue.
limitations: Only a single restart cycle was captured; no additional stress scenarios (e.g., concurrent access, group-based ACL edge cases) were tested, though none were required by the task.
Executor evidence relies on selected command outputs rather than full raw logs, though the provided commands are sufficiently detailed and internally consistent.

operational_hygiene.summary: All state-changing commands map to a clear purpose: directory creation (cmd-35a0be95f9d84d98), two rounds of test-user creation/deletion bracketing functional verification before and after restart (cmd-a64782a0d26a4834, cmd-66b4650d37fb4fa2, cmd-a038126a203c40a9), and explicit cleanup removing test files and users after each round (cmd-bfb29b020d7842df, and the userdel/rm calls embedded in cmd-a038126a203c40a9). The fixed after_executor snapshot confirms no leftover residue (no failed services, no unexpected listening sockets, dpkg healthy, /tmp diff limited to expected systemd-private dirs tied to the reboot itself). userdel's 'mail spool not found' messages are benign. No unnecessary, broad, or destructive mutations were identified.
